concepts.label: Field-Level Encryption (FLE)
concepts.reused_or_minted: minted - JUDGMENT CALL: this is NOT the same thing as the registry's promoted encryption:native-encryption-at-rest. The page states outright 'This is a client-side implementation, with encryption and decryption handled by the Couchbase client SDK' - it encrypts specific JSON document field VALUES inside the application, before the document is sent to Couchbase Server, using application-managed keys (a pluggable Keyring). encryption:native-encryption-at-rest, by contrast, is Couchbase Server encrypting whole buckets/logs/config/audit data ON DISK on the server, using server-managed DEKs protected by encryption:master-password. Different actor (client library vs. server), different scope (named fields vs. whole bucket), different key model (app-supplied Keyring vs. server-managed key hierarchy). Minting a fresh sdk:-scoped id rather than reusing encryption:native-encryption-at-rest or encryption:data-encryption-key, which would be exactly the same-word-different-thing collision the role:* family repeatedly hit.

concepts.reused_or_minted: minted - the pluggable interface FLE uses to obtain encryption keys, with native implementations for Java Key Store and Windows Certificate Store, and custom implementations for external KMS integration/key rotation.

relations.subject: sdk:fle-algorithm
relations.object: the previous Field-Level Encryption algorithm variation that managed AES and HMAC keys separately (SDK 2-era)
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused - the docs position the joined 64-byte-key algorithm as the preferred way forward without asserting the old algorithm has stopped working (it 'can still be read')
relations.evidence: Previous versions of the Field-Level Encryption library used a variation of this algorithm that managed the AES and HMAC keys separately. This was an obstacle to key rotation, so those algorithms are deprecated in SDK 3 and are no longer used for encryption. Existing data encrypted with the old algorithm can still be read by SDK 3, although additional configuration is required to enable backwards compatibility.

relations.evidence: To prevent data loss under error conditions, an error in decryption or encryption in any part of an operation will cause the whole operation to fail with an exception.

notable_absence.finding: This page never mentions Couchbase Server's native/at-rest encryption at all - no comparison, no disambiguation, not even the word 'server-side'. It defines Field-Level Encryption entirely in isolation, purely as a client-side SDK capability. The explicit contrast between the two mechanisms only appears on the paired howto page (encrypting-using-sdk.md), not here - so this concept page alone gives no textual basis for a hasNoRelationshipTo or shouldNotBeConfusedWith triple, even though the two mechanisms are in fact unrelated. Recorded as a gap: a reader landing on this concept page first, without following through to the howto's tip box, has no signal that a completely different 'encryption at rest' feature exists on Server 8.x.

cross_component_finding: The page states plainly that 'Field Level Encryption for all SDKs is a separate package from the Couchbase SDK itself; the APIs are extensions of the SDK, but the SDK does not have a dependency on FLE' - meaning FLE is an optional, separately-versioned add-on library (java-couchbase-encryption) layered on top of the core Java SDK, not a built-in SDK feature. This is a packaging/dependency relationship worth distinguishing from a plain 'is a capability of' relationship, though no existing predicate in the registry cleanly captures 'optional extension package with no reverse dependency' - flagged rather than force-fit.
cross_product_finding: JUDGMENT CALL FOR THE COORDINATOR: per this round's framing, I did NOT reuse encryption:native-encryption-at-rest, encryption:data-encryption-key, or encryption:master-password for anything on this page, and minted sdk:field-level-encryption, sdk:fle-keyring, and sdk:fle-algorithm instead. The determining evidence is the page's own words: 'This is a client-side implementation, with encryption and decryption handled by the Couchbase client SDK' (client-side, field-scoped, app-managed Keyring) versus the registry's encryption:native-encryption-at-rest, defined from server/8.0 pages as 'Couchbase Server's built-in encryption of data on disk' (server-side, whole-bucket-scoped, server-managed DEK/KEK/master-password hierarchy). These are two structurally unrelated mechanisms that happen to share the word 'encryption' - the same collision pattern already seen five times in the role:* family. The explicit docs-stated disambiguation between the two (via howtos/encrypting-using-sdk.md's tip box) is recorded in that page's own extraction record rather than here, since only that page contains the comparative text.
